OK, Ryan — go ahead!

We’re on **question 49** when you’re back: who found it **hard to review** the game?

See you in a minute.
Oh, I know It is speed. It says the challenges of endless endless oceans can be difficult to meet, But this is what makes the game rather intriguing.

Welcome back!

Good find — that line is about the **game’s challenges** being hard.

But **question 49** asks who found it hard to **review** the game (hard to **judge / write about** it) — not hard to **play**.

> Look for words like **challenging to evaluate** / hard to decide what to say about the game.

Try again for **49** — **A, B, C, or D**?
b

Close — **B** has the word “difficult,” but that’s about **playing**, not **reviewing**.

Here’s the review clue:

> From Photo 1, Review C: the game’s slow pace makes it **“challenging to evaluate.”**

**Evaluate** ≈ write a review / decide what you think.

So for **49**, which letter — **B** or **C**?
c

Yes — **C**! “Challenging to **evaluate**” = hard to **review**. You spotted the trap word “difficult” and switched — smart. **49 = C.** ✓

**Question 50:** Who **explains why people like computer games** (the attraction)?

Look for **excitement / missing in everyday life / why people play**.

Which letter — **A, B, C, or D**?
D, because most people who spend a lot of time on computer games admit that they do it to find excitement that missing in their everyday lives.

Yes — **D**! You quoted the exact clue: games for **excitement missing in everyday life**. That’s the **attraction**. **50 = D.** ✓

**Question 51:** Who thinks the game should give **more of a challenge**?

Look for **too easy / doesn’t ask much of the player / needs to be harder**.

Which letter — **A, B, C, or D**?
The next one is  a.

Good — you picked **A** for **51**.

Before I say yes or no: **why A?** What words made you think that reviewer wants a **harder** game?
It says that it's just a shame that the game doesn't make any demands on the player. The demands means the challenges.

Yes — perfect! **“Doesn’t make demands”** = too easy → wants **more challenge**.

**Question 51 = A.** ✓

Last one — **question 52:** Who says the game is **worth playing even with its faults**?

Look for **recommend / give it a go / still worth it** (even after complaining).

Which letter — **A, B, C, or D**?
A, because it has the sentence that was used by questions 51. and it says I'd recommend giving it a go.

Yes — **A**! Same review as **51**, and **“I’d recommend giving it a go”** = worth trying **even with faults**. **52 = A.** ✓

Ryan — you finished **all of Part 7 (43–52)**! You matched clues, caught trap words like “difficult,” and even quoted the text yourself. Proud of that detective work.

Quick check — how sure do you feel on this matching part: **1**, **2**, or **3**?

Nice work finishing that game-review matching, Ryan — and a **4-day streak** too!

These photos look like **vocab homework**: about **20 words** you numbered (from **idiom / ignite / ignore** through **influence**).

We’ll go **one word at a time** — meaning in your own words, then a sentence you invent.

**Where do you want to start — word number 1, or a different number?**

Let’s start with **word 1** — your book marks these three together: **idiom**, **ignite**, **ignore**. We’ll do them one by one.

First up: **idiom**.

> From your book: **idiom** — “习语; 成语” (a set phrase)

Here’s a tiny clue: when someone says **“it’s raining cats and dogs,”** they don’t mean animals are falling from the sky — that’s an **idiom**.

**In your own words, what does idiom mean?**
ignite

Got it — let’s do **ignite**.

> From your book: **ignite** — “点火; 使燃烧; 激起” (light a fire / start something burning / spark a feeling)

Picture this: you strike a match, and the candle **ignites**.

**In your own words, what does ignite mean?**
Can you ignore the Chinese words from my book, and I cannot imagine the word ignite.

No problem, Ryan — we’ll use **English only**, no Chinese from the book.

**Ignite** means **to start a fire** or **make something begin to burn**.

Think of a birthday candle: when the flame touches the wick, the candle **ignites**.

Which picture matches **ignite** best?
- **A)** A candle starts burning
- **B)** A candle melts into a puddle
- **C)** You blow the candle out

Which one — **A, B, or C**?
Can we say we ignite the engine.

Great try, Ryan — you’re thinking of **starting something up**. That’s close!

For a car, we usually say **start the engine**.  
**Ignite** fits better with **fire or fuel** — like a rocket: *The rocket engines ignite.*

Now invent **one short sentence** with **ignite** (candle, match, or rocket — your pick). What will you write?
the stove egnites and the water began to burn

Nice science thinking — you linked **ignite** with a **stove** (fire/heat). That part is on track!

Two tiny fixes to check:
1. Spelling: **ignites** (not “egnites”)
2. Meaning: **water** doesn’t burn — it **boils** / gets hot. The **gas** or **flame** is what ignites.

Try again with your idea — something like: *The stove _____ …*  
What sentence will you write this time?
ignite

You’re sticking with **ignite** — good.

Finish **your** stove idea. Pick the better ending:

**The stove ignites, and…**
- **A)** the water **boils**
- **B)** the water **burns**

Which one — **A or B**?
next word

Okay — **ignite** = **start a fire / begin to burn**. You can keep your sentence: *The stove ignites, and the water boils.* ✓

Next word in your group: **ignore**.

**Ignore** means **to not listen to** or **pretend not to notice** something.

Quick check — which one shows **ignore**?
- **A)** Mom calls you, and you keep playing
- **B)** Mom calls you, and you answer right away

Which one — **A or B**?
practice the spelling

Let’s practice spelling **ignore** — our current word.

Say it in parts: **ig** — **nore**  
Together: **i-g-n-o-r-e**

Type the word **ignore** from memory (no peeking). Ready — what’s your spelling?
ignore

Yes — **ignore** ✓ Perfect spelling!

Quick bonus: earlier you wrote **egnites**. Let’s fix that one too.

Type **ignite** from memory (remember: **ig** — **nite**). What’s your spelling?
ignite

Yes — **ignite** ✓ You fixed the old “egnites” mistake. Nice!

Group 1 spelling wins: **ignore** + **ignite**.

Quick meaning check for **ignore** (we skipped this): Mom calls, you keep playing — is that **A** ignore, or **B** listen?

Which one — **A or B**?
next word

Okay — **ignore** = not listen / pretend not to notice. (Mom calls, you keep playing = **A**.)

**Word 2: illuminate**

**Illuminate** means **to light up** — or **make an idea clearer**.

Picture a dark room: you turn on a lamp, and the light **illuminates** the room.

Which fits **illuminate** better?
- **A)** turn on a light so you can see
- **B)** close the curtains so it gets dark

Which one — **A or B**?
the teacher iluminates her idea

Smart sentence, Ryan — you used the **“make an idea clearer”** meaning. That’s the harder sense of **illuminate**!

One spelling fix: **illuminates** has **two L’s** — **il-lu-mi-nates** (not “iluminates”).

Type it once correctly: **illuminates**. What’s your spelling?
illuminates

Yes — **illuminates** ✓ Two L’s locked in!

Your full sentence: *The teacher illuminates her idea.* ✓

**Word 3: illustrate**

**Illustrate** means **to explain with an example or a picture**.

Which one shows **illustrate**?
- **A)** You draw a picture to explain a story
- **B)** You hide the picture so nobody can see it

Which — **A or B**?
Can you remove the the quizzes, I only do the sentence.

Got it, Ryan — **no more quizzes**. From now on: meaning in a few words, then **you write one sentence**.

**Word 3: illustrate** = explain with a **picture** or an **example**.

Invent one short sentence using **illustrate**. What will you write?
my dad illustrated a book

Nice — **illustrated a book** = drew the pictures. Perfect use of the word!

Tiny polish: start with a capital — **My** dad illustrated a book.

**Word 4: immense** = **huge** / extremely big.

Write one sentence with **immense**. What will you write?

I'm going to do a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit

Ha — that’s a **very long** “little bit,” Ryan!

Sounds like you need a tiny break-brain moment. Ready when you are.

We’re on **word 5: immigrate** = move **into** a new country to live.

One short sentence with **immigrate** — or say **pause** if you want a real break first. Your call?
immigrate

Still stuck on the sentence? That’s okay — let’s shrink it.

Just fill the blank with a country:

**My family will immigrate to ______.**

What country will you put there?
next

Okay — we can skip the sentence for now.

**Immigrate** = move into a new country to live. ✓

**Word 6: implement** = **put a plan into action** / make it happen.

Write one sentence with **implement** — or say **next** again if you want to skip. Your move?
implement

Good — **implement** spelling ✓

Fill the blank (easy mode):

**Our class will implement a plan to ______.**

What will you put in the blank? (or say **next** to skip)
next

Skipping **implement** for now ✓

**Word 7: improvise** = make something up **on the spot** (no plan ready).

Write one sentence with **improvise** — or say **next** to skip. Your call?
this trip is improvise

Cool idea — a trip with **no fixed plan** fits **improvise**!

Tiny fix: use **improvised** (describing the trip), or as a verb: *We had to improvise on this trip.*

Your version: *This trip is improvised.* ✓

**Word 8: impulse** = a **sudden wish** to do something (without thinking long).

Write one sentence with **impulse** — or say **next**. Your call?
impules

Close spelling! It’s **impulse** — **im-pulse** (not “impules”).

Try typing **impulse** once, then a tiny sentence if you want:

**On impulse, I ______.**

What will you write? (or **next**)
impuse

Almost! You’re missing one letter: **L**.

**im-pu-l-se** → **impulse**

Type it with the **L**: **impulse**. Ready?
this is a scar on my feet

Hey Ryan — thanks for showing me! Those little pale spots look like **well-healed scar skin** — smoother and lighter than the skin around them.

Your body is pretty clever: when skin gets hurt, it builds new tissue to close the gap. Sometimes that new skin doesn’t get its full color back, so it stays a bit lighter.

**Quick science question for you:** do you remember roughly how that spot got hurt — a scrape, a cut, or something else?
when can the skin heal

Great science question, Ryan.

Skin **starts healing almost right away** — your body rushes tiny “repair workers” to the spot. A small scrape often closes in about **a few days to a couple of weeks**. A scar’s **color** (like those pale spots) can stay lighter for a long time, even after the cut itself is done healing.

**What if…** you gently touch your scar now — does it still feel sore, or more like ordinary skin?
Ordinary, if by the time I was a grown up, will the spots disappear.

Honest answer, Ryan: **maybe a little**, but often **not completely**.

Those pale spots are healed skin that didn’t get its full color back. As you grow, scars can fade or soften — but many stay as a light mark even when you’re grown up. That doesn’t mean anything’s wrong; it’s just your skin’s “memory” of the repair.

**Quick pick:** would you rather the scar **fade a bit** over years, or stay as a cool “adventure stamp” you can tell a story about?
stay

Love that choice, Ryan — an **adventure stamp** it is.

Your body already finished the hard repair work; the pale spots are just the leftover “mark” of that story. Lots of people keep a scar like a tiny souvenir.

Want to tell me the **one-sentence story** of how it happened? (Or we can switch to math / reading / something else — your call.)

Nice switch — this is **reading with evidence**.
